title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
summary: Exploit Public-Facing Application covers adversary exploitation of weaknesses in internet-reachable software to obtain code execution, data access or a foothold inside a network. The targets are the services an organisation deliberately exposes: web applications and their frameworks, remote access and virtual private network gateways, file transfer and mail servers, content management systems, and the APIs behind them. The mechanism is usually a flaw in input handling, authentication or deserialisation that lets an attacker influence server-side behaviour, but the category also includes misconfiguration such as an exposed administrative interface, a default credential on an appliance, or a debug endpoint left reachable, as well as exploitation of a dependency the application implicitly trusts. Time matters a great deal, because exploitation commonly follows public vulnerability disclosure closely and internet-wide scanning means exposed hosts are probed continuously, so telemetry often shows attempts against many assets rather than one carefully chosen request. The evidence lives in web and reverse proxy access logs, web application firewall and intrusion detection alerts, application error logs, process creation on the host running the service, and network flow records. An investigation must separate attempted exploitation from successful compromise, which requires correlating an anomalous request with a subsequent child process, a new file, an outbound connection or a configuration change on the same asset within a coherent time window. Heavy legitimate traffic, commercial vulnerability scanners and benign crawlers generate enormous volumes of superficially malicious requests, so triage should weight requests that returned a success status, that plausibly reached the vulnerable code path, and that were followed by follow-on activity on the affected host.
objectives: Identify which internet-facing assets and software versions carry exploitation risk and how exposure is verified rather than assumed.
Read web, proxy and application logs to distinguish probing from a request that reached vulnerable code.
Correlate a suspicious request with post-exploitation evidence such as child processes, new files or outbound connections.
Explain how virtual patching, web application firewall rules and rapid patching differ in coverage and operational cost.
Build a prioritisation method that combines exploit availability, exposure and asset criticality.
Write detection logic that keys on exploitation behaviour rather than on attacker-controlled request strings alone.
